title: Programming Fundamentals with Python
topicSummary: Python syntax, control structures, functions, file I/O, object-oriented programming and examples.

content.text: This module introduces Python as the primary programming tool for Urban Informatics.
Objective: Enable you to write programs to process urban data, build reusable logic, and prepare for data analysis and machine learning.
Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language known for readability and simplicity.

items: Data types → int, float, string, list, dict

content.text: 📖 Reading Note: Python is ranked #1 in the TIOBE and IEEE Spectrum programming language indices specifically because of its dominance in data science and AI. In the urban context, tools like ArcGIS Pro (GIS software), SUMO (traffic simulator), and Mesa (agent-based modeling) all expose Python APIs — meaning knowing Python lets you control professional-grade city analysis tools. The f-string syntax used above (f"Hello, {name}") is Python 3.6+ and is the modern, preferred way to format strings.

📖 Reading Note: A real loop use case in urban analytics: After downloading a month of hourly air quality readings from Pune's MPCB monitoring stations (720 rows), a for loop processes each reading: for index, row in df.iterrows(): if row['PM25'] > 60: alert_list.append(row['station']). This automatically generates a list of stations that exceeded the safe AQI threshold — something that would take hours to check manually. This is the foundation of automated environmental monitoring systems.
Definition: Functions are reusable blocks of code that perform a specific task.

📖 Reading Note: The DRY principle (Don't Repeat Yourself) is central to good programming. In urban data pipelines, the same data cleaning steps (drop nulls → fill missing → convert types) are performed on every dataset downloaded. Instead of copying those 10 lines every time, you write it once as a function: def clean_urban_df(df): df = df.drop_duplicates(); df = df.fillna(df.median()); return df. Then call it on any new dataset. Clean, professional, maintainable — exactly how smart city platforms are built.
Definition: File I/O allows programs to read and write data to files.

📖 Reading Note: The 'with open()' pattern (context manager) is important — it automatically closes the file even if an error occurs, preventing data corruption. In urban IoT systems, a common practice is 'log rotation': the firmware writes sensor data to a log file on the device; when the file reaches 1MB, it's compressed, sent to cloud, and a fresh file starts. This File I/O pattern underpins how edge devices (like roadside air quality monitors) manage local data before cloud upload.
Definition: OOP organizes code into objects and classes.
Modeling real-world entities: Vehicles, Sensors, Traffic systems.

📖 Reading Note: OOP makes large systems manageable. Consider a smart city platform that handles 50 types of sensors (temperature, noise, PM2.5, water level, parking…). Instead of 50 separate scripts, you create a base class: class Sensor (id, location, read_data(), send_to_cloud()). Each specific sensor type (class TemperatureSensor(Sensor)) inherits common behavior and only overrides the unique parts (like read_data, which converts analog voltage to Celsius). This is Inheritance — the most powerful OOP concept for scalable sensor management.
Scenario: Analyze traffic speeds and flag violations.
Workflow: Input data → File/API → Process (Loops + conditions) → Organize (Functions / Classes) → Output (Files / dashboards).

content.text: 👉 Using try-except ensures: Program doesn't crash, Errors are handled gracefully.

📖 Reading Note: In a real IoT deployment, unhandled errors are catastrophic. Imagine a Python script running on a Raspberry Pi at a flood monitoring station — if the sensor returns NaN (sensor malfunction) and your code tries to compare NaN > 5.0 without try-except, the entire script crashes and your flood alert system goes silent. Always wrap sensor read operations in try-except with a fallback: except Exception as e: log_error(e); use_last_known_value(). This is called 'fault tolerance' — essential for production urban systems.

Python is the common language used in Week 5 (Pandas), Week 6–9 (scikit-learn, Keras), Week 10–11 (pyserial, MQTT clients), and Week 12 (GeoPandas, Plotly Dash). Mastering Week 4 is the single highest-ROI investment in this course.
